title: Beyond the Code: How to Get Management on Your Side
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni argues that technical professionals fail to win executive support because they lean on logic and data when decisions are driven by emotion and business context. She offers short sections on framing bugs in terms of business consequences, communicating project impact realistically but hopefully, and reframing technical objections as concerns for end users. One anecdote shows her team halting a poor tool purchase by presenting three simple, business-relevant concerns. The central move is to define your objective first and then use social awareness to speak to what leaders want. Aimed at tech workers, but the influence-upward lessons apply to any team leader.
points: Logic and data alone rarely persuade senior leaders; framing an issue in business consequences does.
Realism softened with hope, delivered privately to leaders, beats either doom or cheerleading when reporting a struggling project.
Technical objections gain traction when recast as concerns for end users rather than for the technical team.
Define your goal first, then adapt your message to what motivates each stakeholder.
quotes: But you see, it goes beyond data and facts. Logic can only get you so far here. You have to have management on your side, and it is not by sucking up to them. You have to be strategic to do it

It would help if you framed the bug and why it is important within the business context. For example, a bug makes it so a certain product cannot be billed correctly. If that happens, you will have many angry salespeople potentially not getting the right commissions, a demoralized sales support team, and even worse, potential audits from the government, depending on the industry. See what we did there? There were no numbers, but it struck the emotion in a way the business stakeholders could understand clearly.
The most successful approach has been the middle road of realism yet softening language where applicable. This applies whether you are in a PM role or not. Why? Perception matters for buy-in.

Be real, but also direct. If there is an issue, address it, but also offer room for hope in what can be improved. If the leadership team needs to do something, talk to them privately instead of blasting them with 50+ people.

Data alone being reported, even if favorable, will not be enough to express project impact. You need to control the narrative by painting the story. What is the result the project team is expecting? How will this make life better? This is social awareness, a pillar of emotional intelligence, in action.
I changed the narrative to make the decision business relevant. I asked my team to provide up to 3 of their concerns, which needed to be simple and easily explained.
a mistake to assume that data alone will drive decisions or even what is logical. People think emotionally first, whether they admit it or not.
